utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Tecla Benjamin, Ekkehard Withopf, and the case manager, Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Appearing on behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber bids good morning to all those present, the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, the attorneys, the accused, as well as all the staff of this courtroom, and in particular our new registrar for today. Yesterday during the status hearing, the question was raised regarding the completion of the Prosecution case. It was indicated that the Office of the Prosecutor would comply with the date the 1st of June or beginning of June. The Chamber that reviewed this matter after the hearing wishes to underline that that date which was indicated both during the pre-trial and during the hearings is an approximate date. It cannot be considered as a definitive one; since some witnesses were drawn and others need to be heard subsequently, the Prosecution does have the possibility of calling those witnesses or other witnesses in the course of the month of June. I wish to underline that the 1st of June is not a fixed date for closing the Prosecution case, it was an approximate date. But in view of the presentation of the evidence, the witnesses, and the documents, it is quite possible that this date may be moved by one, two, or three weeks, depending on the needs of the Prosecution. Therefore, we wish to reassure the Prosecution that the 1st of June was just a provisional indication but does not necessarily mean the closing of the case on that particular date. We all have experiences with trials of this kind, and we know that it is very difficult to stick to such fixed deadlines because some witnesses are not available and because of other difficulties that may arise. So it is quite possible to have extensions. And it is the opinion of the Chamber that it should appeal to the parties to accept this indication that the 1st of June is an approximation, and the Chamber is quite prepared to postpone the closing date. So, Mr. Withopf, do you have any remarks to make in that connection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President. As already indicated yesterday, we are currently revisiting our witness list. Due to the fact that a number of anticipated court days couldn't be used, it appears to be likely that the Prosecution will need either the full month of June or portions of the month of June for additional witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. As the Defence has no observations to make, we will begin today's hearing with a witness. And I should like to ask Madam Usher to be kind enough to bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Let me check first that you are hearing the interpretation in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called as a witness for the Prosecution to testify about facts or events which took place in 1993 in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I need first to know your identity, so will you please tell me your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Jasenko Eminovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When were you born, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 29th of September, 1971.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where? In what town or village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am employed in the non-governmental organisation World Vision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1993, that is, more than ten years ago, what were you doing? What was your occupation or position in those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a member of the Municipal Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this municipal commission was in which town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the building? It was in Travnik, in premises close to the municipal building, the town hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you already testified in court, or is this your first time to appear before an international or a national tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my first time, today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I need to hear you read the solemn declaration. Will you be kind enough to do that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to representatives of the Prosecution for your examination-in-chief, it is my duty to give you some information regarding the proceedings here. You will be asked questions by representatives of the Chief Prosecutor and representatives of the Prosecution are on your right. After these questions, which may take one and a half to two hours, you will be asked questions by the Defence attorneys, who are seated to your left. Within the framework of this hearing, the three Judges in front of you may at any point in time ask you questions if they see fit either to clarify the answers you have given or to fill in any gaps that the Judges may notice in the course of your testimony. Furthermore, as you have read the solemn declaration, I need to indicate that this excludes all possibility of lies or false testimony. A witness must know that should he provide false testimony he could be prosecuted for perjury and punished with a fine or a prison sentence or both. Furthermore - but this should not apply to you - if a witness in his replies is prompted to provide evidence which could be used against him, he may refuse to answer. In that case, the Chamber may compel him to answer nevertheless, and the reply given upon the insistence of the Chamber cannot be used to incriminate him but will -- he will be granted certain immunity in that respect. So those would be the general frameworks of this hearing. Try and give full answers to the questions. If you don't understand a question or if it seems to be complicated, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. As this is a purely oral hearing, it is very important that the answers of the witnesses should be clear and precise to inform the Judges properly. Should there be any difficulty of any kind, please let us know and the Judges in front of you will deal with it. I turn now to the representative of the Prosecution, who is going to begin with the examination-in-chief. Madam Benjamin, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Eminovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You indicated to the Trial Chamber that you were born in the village of Travnik. Could you tell us which municipality Travnik is located in, please.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you give the Trial Chamber a breakdown of the ethnic composition of your village of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Travnik is not a village. It's a town.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Correction, the town of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me about the population composition before the war?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, before the war there was roughly an equal number of Bosniaks and Croats, perhaps slightly more Bosniaks, in the territory of Travnik municipality and about 20 or so per cent were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, could you tell us the relationship that existed among the villagers in the town of Travnik prior to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I can speak about my own relationships and my immediate family members' with the people of other ethnicities. And in those days, we had highly harmonious relations. We socialised. And there were no problems whatsoever linked to anybody's ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Eminovic. Could you state for the Trial Chamber if you did compulsory service with the JNA and for what period, please.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I did not do my compulsory military service in the JNA, but I completed the military secondary school from 1986 to 1990, and I attended the military academy anti-aircraft defence department from 1990 to 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Aside from your service in 1990 to 1992, subsequent to that, were you enlisted or registered in any other military body or any -- did you work for any service?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was a member of the reserve force of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and a member of the Municipal Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, could you, then, tell the Trial Chamber what was your rank then and your duties.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: In that period I had no rank. And in the Commission for Exchanges, I prepared lists of POWs. I prepared their exchange. I worked on a database for missing persons from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I took statements from persons expelled from the region of Bosanska Krajina regarding the circumstances of war crimes and genocide. Those would roughly be my activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying, then, that your duties were basically of an administrative nature?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you please state for the Trial Chamber who or whom were you subordinated to.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I was subordinated to Salko Beba, who was the president of the municipal exchange commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And do you know who Salko Beba was subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Salko was subordinated to the state Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, could you please describe for the Trial Chamber what took place in particular to Guca Gora during your tenure with the commission. Could you tell us some of your observations, please. And sorry, between January 1993 to March 1994. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, nothing was happening in Guca Gora from January -- no, sorry. Sorry. Sometime in the summer of 1993, Salko Beba and I went to Guca Gora and we saw that at the monastery in Guca Gora there were some inscriptions in Arabic. We received that information, I don't remember from whom, and we tried to paint over those graffiti in white so that the priests in the monastery would not suffer mentally because of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you elaborate for us what was your reason for going to the monastery.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: We had received information that the monastery had been desecrated; I don't know from whom. We got into a car and went up there, and we saw the graffiti in Arabic. After that, we took some paint and started to paint over those graffiti.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Aside from the monastery, would you be able to assist the Trial Chamber with what Guca Gora looked like to you during that period. How did it appear?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: The road between Travnik and Guca Gora was covered by HVO fire, which means that there was shooting along the road. And upon arrival in Guca Gora, I saw smoke coming from a couple of houses. I saw members of the 306th Brigade securing the monastery.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Specifically to the Croat area in Guca Gora, would you be able to assist us with how the area looked?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Guca Gora is a Croatian village, and to the best of my knowledge it was 100 per cent Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you describe the terrain for us, the village during the period summer 1993, during the conflict. How did the village look to you?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: As I said a moment ago, it looked as usual, except for the fact there was smoke coming from two or three houses and that the monastery had been damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: From your experience, could you tell the Trial Chamber: In the town of Travnik, were you able to see different military bodies? Were they active in the town of Travnik? Were there any military bodies active in the town of Travnik in 1993?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, the command of the 17th Krajina Brigade was based in Travnik, the command of the operations group as well. The command of the 312th Brigade too.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And in particular, any other military bodies or any other bodies that --

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I'm going to be specific. Have you ever heard the term "Mujahedins"?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Do you know what a Mujahedin looks like?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as what I saw is concerned, they were citizens of different countries. They wore beards, and their trousers were ankle length.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And did you see these people in the summer of 1993 in the town of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So in fact you did see other military bodies, other bodies besides the 306th and -- you saw Mujahedin, did you?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: They were not members of the military organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need for me to object because the question referred to something the witness hadn't said. However, the witness himself has responded adequately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I accept what my friend says, even though I disagree, but I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: While you were a member of the commission, as far as you know, were there any investigations carried out into the beatings of any prisoners at all?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is -- this concludes the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Benjamin. The Judges will have questions, but we will put our questions at the end of the cross-examination. I give the floor to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would kindly ask you to give me more time than was used by the Prosecution, since I prepared my questions on the basis of previous statements and a conversation that I had with the witness while preparing for this trial. So I would like to ask you to grant me more time than the Prosecution used for their examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Eminovic, good morning. As you know, I am Edina Residovic and I am representing General Enver Hadzihasanovic. Is it true that you gave your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 11th and 14th of November, 2003?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a statement that you signed in English, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that we met in Sarajevo last week?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We spoke about what you knew during your stay in Travnik in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to a question from my learned friend, you just said that in 1993 you were mobilised to the reserve force of the police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The reserve police force was within the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina and it was directly subordinated to the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Within the framework of the Ministry of the Interior, there was the public and state security services; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, the State Security Service collected information about war crimes committed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to a question from my learned friend, you said that you became a member of the Commission for Exchange in Travnik municipality in 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I became a member in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Then I misheard. So in 1992. You were appointed to that position by the War Presidency of Travnik municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The War Presidency in Travnik acted as the municipal assembly and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was an organ of civilian authority; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The War Presidency formed a Commission for Exchange in accordance with a decision of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina dated 1992, whereby a state commission was organised at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And it was decided that similar commissions should be formed in the municipalities. Was that the basis for the formation of your own commission?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the activities you engaged in, you know that in mid-1993 in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina bodies were set up which were designed to take care of the exchange of killed and captured members of the army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the state commission, you cooperated with the commission formed within the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Answering questions by my learned friend, you said that Salko Beba was president of this state commission for the municipality of Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Salko Beba was at the same time an employee in the State Security Service of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was in the process of formation in 1993, is it true, Mr. Eminovic, that internal affairs bodies - that is, the police - endeavoured in various ways, in terms of personnel and finance, to assist in training security organs and the military police within the brigades and the operative group in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that sometime in mid-1993, Salko Beba in addition to the duties he had that you mentioned, also took over a part of the duties in the security organ of the Operative Group Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that after that period of time, in view of the fact that you worked with him in the state commission as part of the cooperation between MUP and the security organs, you also assisted him in some of his activities linked to the Operations Group Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you assisted Salko Beba in a part of his duties, you were able to learn of certain orders issued by the corps demanding strict observance of the Geneva Conventions and the protection of the civilian population and religious sites. Within the framework of the activities you engaged in on behalf of Salko Beba, did you have any such knowledge about these things?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true, Mr. Eminovic, that the security organs and the military police of the operations group endeavoured to implement or comply with those orders as much as possible? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown two documents, please, which have been identified. 63 ID, a document of the Defence, and 65 ID [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have been mentioned -- 63 and 65 ID. I believe that you said 64 ID.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 64 ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 64 ID. So it's 64 and 65 ID.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, could you please look at these two documents. Mr. Eminovic, are these orders which you learnt about when partially assisting Mr. Salko Beba within the frameworks of the security bodies?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since the witness has recognised the documents and pronounced himself about them, I think it is the right time to give these documents a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please, Madam Usher, bring these documents to us. So there is document ID 64, an order coming from the 3rd Corps of June 10th, 1993: "Measures against looting and destruction of properties." And document of June 19, 65, which has to do with the arrest of civilians, destruction, looting of property. So which -- what are the observations of the Prosecution concerning these two documents which have been recognised by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And which have been in fact taken by the Office of the Prosecution, because they have a number. 64 will become definitive, and 65, definitive, both concerning the B/C/S version and the English translation. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to the Prosecution, you said that your job - I apologise, that is the question of the President - you said that you worked in the Commission for Exchange in a building near the municipality building. Can I interpret you correctly when you say that after being appointed to the security service of the operations group, Salko Beba also had an office within the JNA barracks in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that you by helping Salko Beba occasionally, when need be, you also -- you would also come to his office in -- within the frameworks of the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that in your statement to the Prosecution you said that on one occasion you saw some soldiers who had arrested a Croat prisoner -- a prisoner and that they exerted force against him?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was Krunoslav Bonic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you prevented the soldiers from mistreating this HVO member and that at the time the soldiers had told you that they had caught him -- captured him during the fighting and that he had in his bag the ears of one of their fighters who had been previously killed? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you had taken Mr. Bonic in order to protect him from the frustrated soldiers and to take from him a statement about the circumstances of his capture and about what he had been told by the mentioned soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that that prisoner, the HVO soldier, did he personally tell you that the HVO paid every soldier 200 German marks if he brought the ears or any part of the bodies of one of the enemy soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I was told 200 for the ears. I don't know about the other parts of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you submitted this answer to the State Security and that subsequently criminal charges had been brought against Bonic?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Personally -- you did not personally charge the soldier who mistreated Bonic because you thought that he did this in a moment of passion and that you by your action, you prevented any infliction of injury to that soldier.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Eminovic, that as part of your duties in the commission, that you were bound by the Geneva Conventions and by the orders issued by the state bodies, military bodies as well, in the sense of collection of information about possible commission of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to the answer of the -- to a question of the Prosecution, you said that you had basically been collecting information from people that had been expelled or exchanged in the territory of Bosanska Krajina, that is, persons that had been expelled by the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will I interpret you correctly if I say that in your statement to the Prosecution you mentioned one of these cases, the killing of about 200 prisoners in Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Eminovic, that at the time in Travnik there were very few people who knew anything about the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was very difficult to come to the text of the Geneva Conventions and for quite some time there was no need for its implementation; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, some information about the Geneva Conventions you had received while you were at the military high school and the military academy, and you had been engaged to lecture and train about the Geneva Conventions to the military police of the Operations Group Bosanska Krajina; is that so?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In so doing, you used some documents that were submitted to the operations group and the brigade by the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Eminovic, that your work as well as the work of the security-service bodies evolved under very difficult conditions? Could you -- is it true that you used documents which were submitted to the operations group and the brigade given by the 3rd Corps? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Eminovic, that all these duties were carried out under very difficult conditions when we had -- when you had no material for taking statements? There was no paper, and very often you did this by hand.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Eminovic, that from all persons who knew about the commission of war crimes, did you take statements from them in the same way; but since most of the people coming to Travnik who were expelled Bosniaks, these statements were taken from the Bosniaks who had such knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecution asked you about your visit to Guca Gora. I would like to ask you, since you told the Prosecution that you don't know from where you received the information about the desecration of the convent, can you tell -- monastery -- do you know whether the Croat mass media published information as to the burning of the monastery? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Until then, I hadn't access to the mass media. But photographs of the monastery had been published in some of the Croatian papers. I saw that afterwards in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The information that you received about the monastery, Salko Beba reacted to that information as assistant security person, and you went along with him in that capacity and not in the capacity of a member of the commission; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In front of the monastery, as you said, you saw members of the 306th Brigade. Was that the military police of the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, yes, they were securing the monastery.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that you saw graffiti on the walls in Arabic script. Is it true that the military police had informed you that that graffiti and the damages onto the monastery were carried out by the Mujahedin and that they were ordered subsequently to secure and safeguard the monastery?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to the question of the Prosecution, you saw that some -- from some of the houses in Guca Gora smoke was coming out. You didn't know who had set fire to these houses and when this had taken place.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In carrying out the orders that you confirmed having seen, you knew that the military police had been securing the church in Travnik. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that when carrying out orders about protection of property, the military police and the security bodies where Mr. Salko was employed in 1993 pressed several scores of criminal charges against people who had been destroying property and carrying out -- committing other crimes to the detriment of the Croat population? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that this had been done, been -- carried out by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Eminovic, that at the time you personally working as a member of the state commission and partially as a member of the reserve forces, you did not press criminal charges for war crimes for some members of the army because you never had any knowledge that the members of the army had carried out such offences?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Eminovic. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Judges are going to ask you a few questions for the sake of clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I should like the know exactly what your position was in relation to the 3rd Corps. You said at the beginning that you were appointed to the reserve force of the Ministry of the Interior and that you were assigned to the Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners, depending on the municipality. And then later on during the questions put to you by the Prosecution and the Defence, we find that you were the deputy of Salko Beba who himself was the deputy commander of the Operations Group Krajina. So it would appear, according to what emerged, that there was a mixture between civilian and military activities. So could you please clarify your position in relation to the military of the BiH. When you were performing your duties in the exchange commission, were you in uniform or were you wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: When I was working in the exchange commission, I wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And when you assisted the army, you were in civilian clothes or in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: In military uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There we are. You have in front of you professional Judges who are accustomed to the testimony of witnesses, and we noticed from the beginning that you were very reticent in answering questions and you limited to -- yourself to giving minimum answers. Now we are moving forward, and we learn now that you were at times wearing military uniform. And when you were in those clothes, who were you subordinated to in the military chain of command?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Salko Beba.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what rank did Salko Beba have in the army?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't have a rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he was wearing military uniform?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, when he was working in the operations group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when he was in the operations group -- and you worked with him within this operations group, didn't you? You worked with him.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you yourself contribute to the drafting of military-type orders?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: As I said earlier on, I assisted him mostly in administrative work. And very rarely did I go into the field - almost never - with members of the army. This was more assistance in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you -- when you went to Guca Gora with him, that was within a military context and not a civilian one, was it?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You answered a question from the Defence by saying -- or rather, confirming a very long question, and that is that it was the military police that informed you that there were inscriptions written by the Mujahedin. Is that what you said a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: That is what I said just now, that military policemen and the priest told us that it had been done by the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because you talked to the priest who was present; right?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I just exchanged greetings with him, and then Salko Beba continued to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the priest, did he demand that the person who did this should be identified? What did the priest say to Salko Beba that you overheard?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't present. I went to paint over the walls. But as far as I can remember, Salko Beba went inside with the priest into the monastery. So I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As part of your duty which appeared to be of an intellectual nature, it seems to be astonishing that someone of your level with the military academy should take a brush and a pot of paint to paint over an inscription. Did you do this upon an order given to you or spontaneously, of your own free will?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I did so of my own free will, as I was brought up to believe that nobody should suffer mental pain. Nobody should be made to suffer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that means that when you came to Guca Gora you didn't come on foot, obviously; you came in a vehicle. And in this vehicle, there was a pot of paint and a brush? Where did the paint come from? I wish to remind you that you have taken Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the solemn declaration to tell the whole truth. Where did the paint come from?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Some 15 days prior to this incident, Salko Beba and I had been painting the office of the municipal exchange commission and the pot of paint was left behind, and we put this paint into the boot of the car and drove to the monastery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to trouble you with questions which would indicate the opposite of what you're just saying. So you're telling us that you put a pot of paint in the car, which means that when you were on your way there one of you, at least, knew that something needed to be painted. Is that what we need to gather from what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Salko Beba knew that the graffiti had been written and we immediately set off. We knew that the monastery had been desecrated. I don't know where the information had come from but we had that information, that this had been done at the monastery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Another question in another area: You said a moment ago that you were working in a non-governmental organisation. What are you actually doing now?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I am now working in a non-governmental organisation called World Vision, and I am the head of their office in Sarajevo. It's an organisation which engages in aid and development in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this organisation is financed on what basis? You're an employee, a remunerated employee of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a non- -- international non-governmental organisation financed through international grants and private donations worldwide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Another point that may not be clear: You told us that you attended the military academy, and one may wonder why upon completing military academy you did not become a full military officer. Why were you not integrated in the armed forces directly as a military man? Whereas through your answers we learn that you wore a uniform only occasionally. How come that upon leaving the military academy you did not become a full military officer?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't complete the military academy. The war interrupted my education. I was on my second year of the academy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But had you completed the full course at the academy, what rank would you have received?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I would like to ask you some additional questions on what you said this morning. I understand you had two different functions: On the one hand, you were engaged in the exchange of prisoners of war; and on the other hand, you were -- did also other things for the benefit of Mr. Beba, as a sort of assistant to him. Now, the first aspect of what you did in 1993 was you were engaged in the exchange of prisoners between the warring parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did this mainly concern exchanges between Croatian army and official Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Mostly we dealt with the exchange of prisoners of war and taking care of persons expelled from Bosnian Krajina, and exchange of prisoners between the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You were based in Travnik. What kind of troops -- Serbian troops were engaged there? What kind of prisoners from the Serbians, the Serbian army, did you have?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Around Travnik several brigades of the Army of Republika Srpska were deployed, and there would be prisoners from the Army of Republika Srpska who were from the broader area of Travnik municipality; and then there were exchanges between the Army of Republika Srpska -- or rather, no, not -- between the presidents of the Commissions for Exchange of Republika Srpska and our own commission. However, the greatest part of the activities had to do with taking care of people expelled from Bosanska Krajina. Also, prisoners of war, members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, may have been captured on other fronts and they would also be exchanged in Travnik. So there were exchanges of prisoners from Batkovic camp, Omarska, Keraterm, and there were even some from Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So this covered a large part of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Officially not, but because there was cooperation between exchange commissions that was well developed, it was easiest to carry out the exchanges in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And the prisoners that you exchanged, that you brought to the other party in exchange for prisoners from the other party, were they -- these prisoners detained in Travnik or other parts of the area dominated by the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Very rarely were they detained in Travnik -- or rather, I have no knowledge of that because there was no such institution in Travnik. Prisoners of war came from the prison in Zenica, the KP Dom. They were escorted by the military police to the place of the exchange and also accompanied by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Were there other places where they came from? You said Zenica and you said -- well, mainly Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were no other places except Zenica. But the bodies of killed fighters were exchanged in any places. They were usually kept in places where there were necessary conditions for that, large refrigeration units in hospitals. So we did our best to exchange bodies of killed fighters as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Before prisoners of war were being exchanged by the Bosnian army or by the other party, did you interview them yourself? Did you have any meetings with them?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: No. This was done by the military security bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So you didn't see them physically.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I would see them physically when they were actually being exchanged, or rather, transported to the spot where they would be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Would there be reports about them, about their condition or about other circumstances concerning them?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: They were registered by the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you read the reports on them?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have access to such reports, as that was the discretionary right of the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You said that to your knowledge there were no prisoners of war detained in Travnik. Nevertheless, you told us about a certain Croatian soldier, Bonic, whom you met, if I understood you well, in the barracks of Travnik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: He was detained. And as soon as charges were put, he was transferred to the Zenica prison. He wasn't held there for any length of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But you saw him in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And this was in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: What was the occasion when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: He was arrested that same day, and ears were found on him, ears that had been cut off from the head of a Bosnian army fighter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: In what capacity were you in the barracks when you saw this incident?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I was assisting Salko Beba. I was in the office of Mr. Salko Beba and we received information that a member of the HVO, a 16-year-old boy, had been arrested on whom ears had been found that had been cut off of a Bosnian combatant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you often go to the barracks in order to meet Mr. Beba or did you have a room of your own there?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have a room of my own there. It would most often be once or twice a week when I would spend a couple of hours in the premises of the exchange commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Was the exchange commission sitting -- having a seat there in the JNA barracks in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: No. The exchange commission was accommodated in a building some 50 metres from the municipal building in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Then I do not quite understand your reason for visiting the barracks. You said you were there to meet -- to have a meeting with Beba. You mentioned in this respect the exchange commission. But the exchange commission was having a seat somewhere else. So please explain to me what were -- what was the purpose of your visit to Beba in the JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: To discuss future activities linked to the exchange commission; to assist him in administrative work linked to his own work in the operations group, to exchange information with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you -- when you were visiting Beba in the JNA barracks, did you have other contacts with other prisoners who were held there?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: How came it that you saw the incident about Bonic?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Because I received information. I was in Beba's office at the time. One of the combatants came and told us that this man had been arrested, and I went immediately to the detention place to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So you were aware that prisoners of war were being held in the JNA barracks. Bonic was an example.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Bonic was the first example that I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But his presence indicated that there were prisoners of war there, or -- isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you, because that day, probably an hour or an hour and a half before that, he had been arrested and it was not possible to transport him anywhere else except there. So probably that was the safest place to keep him until he was transported to the Zenica prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Are you saying in effect that you were not aware of other prisoners of war in Travnik at the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: No. They may have been kept there for a day or two until statements were taken from them. And as soon as criminal charges were put, they would be transported to Zenica. Because this wasn't a prison; this was a detention on remand, a temporary detention area and it was of such a capacity that it couldn't be used as a prison. It was mostly used to accommodate members of the army who had committed offences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You said that besides being engaged in the exchange of prisoners you also did other things for Mr. Beba. On questions of the President, you told us also that on occasion you had a military uniform. Could you tell us something more about the other functions you fulfilled as an assistant to Mr. Beba. My first question is: Were you appointed officially as an assistant?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't appointed officially as his assistant, nor as a member of the operations group. I was a member of the exchange commission. And as the operations group did not have sufficient capability at the time, they needed assistance of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So this was a practical agreement between Mr. Beba and you, or between the exchange commission and Mr. Beba.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Between me and Mr. Beba.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: How much time did it take, this work for Mr. Beba?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: You mean in the operations group?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: On average each week.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: In the exchange commission, I spent most of my time. A couple of times during the week we would meet in the operations group. We would spend a couple of hours working together on administrative matters in which he needed assistance. There were no working hours during the war. There were days when we worked for 20 hours on end, and there were others when we worked less, but never less than 12 or 13 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I do not get a clear picture, I must say. I was simply asking you how much part of your time were you doing for -- work for Mr. Beba in another capacity, then, as a member of assistant of the exchange commission. What was the most important part of your work?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I understand the question now. A moment ago the question wasn't so clear to me; that is why my answer wasn't so clear. I said that I worked for a couple of hours two or three times a week with Mr. Beba, linked to matters in the operations group. These were administrative matters such as the writing of orders; organisation of transports or something like that; work on training members of the military police company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And this was the capacity under which you and Beba visits Guca Gora? You were not there as a member of the exchange of prisoners commission, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You said something about drawing orders for Mr. Beba. What kind of orders could that be?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: These were mainly orders relating to the activities of the military police company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, it may be the time for a break. The Prosecution, however, very respectfully, due to the answers the witness has given in cross-examination, asks for a longer break of maybe one and a half hours, please, to prepare for the re-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Withopf, you would like a one and a half hour break or a half-hour break?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If possible - and I think it should be possible, since there's no other witness scheduled for today - at least an hour. There are a number of issues that came up in cross-examination we have to address in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will resume the hearing at half past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges will continue with their questions. I give the floor, therefore, to Judge Swart, who will continue with his questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: We were discussing your activities as an assistant of Mr. Beba before the break, and you said, among other things, that you were doing administrative work for him, and as an example you mentioned the drafting of orders for the military police. My next question would be: Have you also been involved in drafting reports for Mr. Beba?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Have you been engaged in drafting correspondence for Mr. Beba?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: What do you remember of your activities in general, apart from drafting orders?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to that, we would discuss the activities of the exchange commission. In those days, there was a large influx of refugees and exiles from the region of Bosnian Krajina. And we agreed on our cooperation with UNPROFOR, with the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You said before the break that you were engaged in work for Mr. Beba apart from your role as a participant in the exchange commission for prisoners. And you said that each week -- or each now and then you spent a number of hours working for Mr. Beba on another topic than related to the exchange of prisoners. And that's what my question is about. As an example, you mentioned drafting orders for the military police. And my question is: What else?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I said that several times during the week I would spend two or three hours a day working with Mr. Beba. In addition to orders, I was involved in the training of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Some other things?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So drafting orders and teaching the military police. That was your activities for Mr. Beba, apart from the exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Tell me -- thank you. Tell me something more about your teaching job. You teached the international humanitarian law, the Convention of Geneva, to the military police. How many military policemen did you teach? In what period? For how long? Tell us something about it.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: This was the teaching of military police from the crime department of the military police company. So there were about four or five military policemen in that department who had higher qualifications and who collected information. They took statements from witnesses. They collected information about criminal activities by members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In addition to that, I also engaged in teaching them about military topography and infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So all in all you teached some four or five members of the military police, higher-ranking persons within the hierarchy. How many lessons did you give them on international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: All in all, this was about ten hours of work with them, regarding those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You mean solely on the law of war? Not also on the other topics you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Just the laws of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: What was the purpose of your teaching them international humanitarian law? Was it to interview persons who had been expelled from other parts of Bosnia, or were there other reasons?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose was for them to be able to perform their duties as professionally as possible in accordance with standards and without any prejudice when it came to collecting information; making sure they had respect for the person they were interviewing, that they wouldn't humiliate them, regardless of whether it was a member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or a member of some other military forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Do you know other things about teaching international humanitarian law to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Were there many teachers like you, or were you the only one?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: For these policemen, I was the one who taught them; that is, the four or five policemen. As for others, I don't know. I know that there was an order issued by the 3rd Corps on respect for the Geneva Conventions and the laws and customs of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: To come back to something else that you said before Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the break. You mentioned the drafting of orders demanding respect for the Geneva Conventions, and you said at a given moment - if I have noted down it correctly; otherwise, you should correct me - that to your knowledge the security agencies and military police endeavoured to implement and comply with those orders as much as possible. Is that a correct statement of what you said?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: A little bit later you mentioned as an example Guca Gora, where you have witnessed the fact that the church there, which you had visited, was protected by the Bosnian army against new violations, I suppose. My question is the following: Your statement is very general and you have given an example of Guca Gora. Do you know about other examples?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: The Catholic church in Travnik was also under the protection of the military and civilian police in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Have you witnessed that or do you know that from another source?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I saw it in passing. I saw members of the military and civilian police guarding the Catholic church in Travnik. The church is in the centre of town. So that all passers-by could see that it was being guarded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But your statement is more general than the protection of cultural property; or isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So please explain. How do you know about the other aspects of respect for international humanitarian law? For example, the treatment of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I was engaged teaching these four or five military policemen as to how a statement should be taken professionally, without any kind of bias or without trying to treat a captured member of a different force in any other way except as provided for by the Geneva Conventions. The training was done in such a way that prisoners of war should be given protection. Statements should be taken from them regarding the events and the circumstances surrounding a war crime, and that the proceedings should be continued in accordance with the law. At the same time, it was emphasised that prisoners of war must be registered by the International Red Cross and that they should be able to communicate freely with representatives of the International Red Cross at all times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But that, Witness, is the theory, and you know that as well as I do. It doesn't necessarily say that the practice is in conformity. And that was what your statement implied. You said - and this is also why I ask this - that you were doing administrative work. If you're doing administrative work, then the question arises: How did you know that the practice is in conformity with international law? You don't need to comment on this, but if you want to, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the practice is concerned, I didn't have access to all information linked to activities on the ground, so I cannot confirm this. But confirmation of what I saw was what I saw in Guca Gora and the church in Travnik. These are things that I witnessed with my own eyes, and there's no dilemma about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Eminovic, I must remind you that you have pled to tell the whole truth. And when you're asked a question, you will tell us the truth. I have a few more remaining questions for you. Within the framework of the exchange of prisoners, was there an instance when during the prisoner exchange you learnt of Mujahedin prisoners being exchanged for HVO soldiers? Were there any exchanges of that type to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us that all prisoner exchanges that you contributed to or you were involved in had to do solely either with soldiers of the BH army or soldiers of the HVO. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: And soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska. Most of them, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in most cases, you had exchanges for Serb prisoners; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, as far as you know, according to you there were never exchanges of HVO soldiers for foreigners.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I shall now give the floor to the Defence for their questions. I shall also give the floor to the Prosecution. I must recall that the Appeals Chamber recently rendered a decision regarding the refreshment of the memory of a witness. When a witness forgets passages from his written statement, then the Prosecution may show him that written statement to jog his memory. And if it is a hostile witness, then the Prosecution is entitled to submit all previous statements given by that witness. This is a ruling of the Appeals Chamber rendered a short while ago. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. With your permission, the Defence would like to address the Chamber in the absence of the witness in connection with the ruling of the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Usher, will you take the witness out for a few minutes, and let him be nearby, because we will bring him back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In order to avoid all misunderstanding during the re-examination of the witness that we have here this morning, I would simply like to say concerning the decision of the Appeals Chamber, which is clear and says that a prior statement given to the investigators may be used to refresh the memory of the witness, Mr. President, in the opinion of the Defence that is quite different from trying to contradict the witness using his statement. To refresh his memory means that the witness doesn't remember a particular point, and then his statement can be shown to him to tell him, "Have you forgotten this fact?" But one cannot use that statement to contradict what the witness has said. So to avoid any difficulty with the examination of this witness, we wanted to mention this fact before the re-examination of the witness begins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Please, Madam Usher, bring the witness in, and I shall give the floor to Mr. Withopf now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, my colleague, Mrs. Benjamin, will do the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Regarding what the Defence has just said, the Prosecution has no observations to make? If you do, we would have to ask the witness to leave again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I actually wish to make some observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's only for a few more seconds, but that is the procedure. The comment must be made in your absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Withopf. You heard the interpretation given by the Defence regarding the Appeals Chamber ruling, that is, that one can only produce a statement to refresh the memory of a witness, to remind him of a certain fact, but not to contradict what he may be saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, in your introductory remarks, you very accurately combined the issue of a hostile witness and the issue of refreshing the memory of a witness. Of course the Prosecution can - and the Prosecution disagrees with the views of the Defence - can, once a witness is declared hostile, can use his previous statement not only for the purpose to refresh his memory but also to show contradictions between the statement and the today's testimony. This is a very different situation. If the Prosecution in the course of the re-examination decides to declare this witness being a hostile witness, the purpose of showing him his statement will not only be to refresh his memory but also to show him contradictions to his statement and to raise any issues in respect to the witness's credibility. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, regarding a hostile witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague is right. If a witness is declared hostile, according to the common-law procedure one can contradict him with his statement. But declaring a witness hostile is a decision that has to be made by the Chamber at the request of the party bringing that witness and it must say why that witness is a hostile witness. And following such a declaration by the Chamber, the rules change. However, in the opinion of the Defence, this witness is not hostile and until he is declared a hostile witness, his statement may only be used to refresh his memory, to tell him whether he remembers a thing or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there any additional comment regarding these remarks by the Defence, who tell us that if the Prosecution believes that a witness is a hostile one, he has to convey that to the Chamber, which will then declare the witness hostile; and then the Prosecution is authorised to show him the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this actually reflects the procedure that has to be followed. And if and when the Prosecution makes his decision to orally apply for the Chamber to decide that the witness is hostile, the Prosecution will do so, if and when the situation arises. But afterwards, the Prosecution can use the statement to contradict the witness and to ask questions in respect to his credibility -- can actually cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the Chamber notes that everyone agrees. So we will ask Madam Usher to bring the witness back into the courtroom. Regarding the questions put by the Judges, I shall give the floor to the Prosecution, if they have any questions, and then the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Benjamin, in light of the questions put by the Chamber and in the light of the replies given by the witness, do you have any additional questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, with respect to your office or your room with Mr. Beba at the barracks, would you be able to elaborate for the Trial Chamber: How close was the Travnik barracks to where you were located?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: The question is not quite clear to me. The office of the exchange commission was about 20 to 30 minutes away from the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: My question now would be: During your tenure - and I talk specifically from January 1993 to March 1994 - were you familiar with the Travnik prison or detention centre, as you prefer to call it?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the period of mid-1993, when I was in contact with the operations group, until February 1994, I was aware of the fact that in the barracks in Travnik there existed a military detention centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: My question, then, to you would be: Being aware of the detention centre, as you say, was the case of Mr. Bonic the first case that you had known or seen at the detention centre? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was approximately the first time that I went to that detention centre, that I entered the premises of the detention centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Subsequent to Mr. Bonic, would you be able to assist the Trial Chamber as to if there were other prisoners housed at that prison or detention centre, as you prefer to call it.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were members of the ABiH army who were in fact charged with criminal activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Aside from the members of the ABiH army, were there any other prisoners of any other army held in that detention centre?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see them, although I heard that there were some people -- members, that is, imprisoned HVO members who were awaiting transfer to the prison in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And as far as you know, did you receive any reports in your capacity as -- as making recommendations and dealing with exchange of prisoners, did you receive any reports with respect to those that you said you heard of, those HVO prisoners that you had heard of? Did you receive any reports on them in that centre?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't make any recommendations. The exchanges were carried out on request by the HVO exchange commission or the commission of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: With --

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: But I didn't receive any reports about that particular centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: With all due respect to you, Mr. Eminovic, I think you misunderstood the question. My question was: Did you in your capacity receive any reports with respect to prisoners, HVO prisoners, who were held at that detention centre in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I'll be a little more specific. Did you ever hear about beatings of HVO prisoners in the detention centre in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, people were mentioning that, but I hadn't actually witnessed that until the Bonic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You indicated to the Trial Chamber that you yourself had seen the detention centre, the prison. Would you be able to tell the Trial Chamber as to approximately how many prisoners were held in that detention centre at any particular time?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the premises of the prison had two or three rooms. And as far as I could gather, it would not be possible to house more than about ten people in that centre. I don't believe there were more than about 20 people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, as far as you know, as far as what you told us a while ago, these would have been ABiH prisoners, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the purpose of the detention centre, that the members of the ABiH who had committed the criminal acts should remain there until the investigation was completed. The conditions for accommodation were such that people were not able to remain there any length of time; that was on the basis of what I saw in the premises mentioned.
